content_voiceover: This slide covers the reagent side of antibody screening, the indirect antiglobulin test. Screening cells are commercially prepared group O red cells, chosen specifically because O cells lack A and B antigens, so any agglutination you see is due to an unexpected, clinically significant alloantibody, not anti-A or anti-B. Three screening cell panels, SI, SII, and SIII, are selected to express different combinations of Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd, Lewis, MNS, P, and other antigens, so that reacting against one but not another narrows down antibody specificity. A key, high-yield fact for Taiwan-based practice: the local reagent panel includes Mia and Dia positive cells, since these are clinically relevant in the Asian population, but it lacks big K positive cells, because K antigen is rare here. Methods to detect a positive reaction include the antiglobulin tube test, the antiglobulin gel test using an AHG card, and the manual polybrene test.
keypoints: Screening cells are group O, so reactions reflect non-ABO alloantibodies only.
Three-cell panel (SI, SII, SIII) has differing antigen profiles to help identify antibody specificity.
Taiwan reagent panel includes Mia and Dia positive cells but no big K positive cells.
Detection methods: AHG tube test, AHG gel card, or manual polybrene test.
